https://if.com.au/kuba-dorabialskis-agat.text: ADVERTISEMENT Kuba Dorabialski’s ‘Agata the Writer’ selected for Venice’s Giornate degli Autori Mia Wasikowska in 'Agata the Writer'. Agata the Writer , the debut feature from Polish-born Australian visual artist and filmmaker Kuba Dorabialski, will have its world premiere in Venice Film Festival sidebar Giornate degli Autori. It marks the first Australian title selected for the independent parallel section, also known in English as Venice Days, since Ben Young’s Hounds of Love in 2016. Mia Wasikowska leads the film as a Polish-Australian satirical novelist who travels from Sydney to Sarajevo to write a war novel. While in Bosnia she finds herself within a startling mystery, forcing her to question her role as a storyteller. The film is one of 10 in competition, with the all-female jury headed by Spanish director Carla Simón. Dorabialski, based in Sydney, is known for an art practice that bridges gallery-based video installation and cinema. In addition to writing and directing, he also served as Agata the Writer ‘s cinematographer, editor and composer. Alex White, whose film Babyteeth premiered in official competition at the Venice Film Festival in 2019 , is the producer. “It is an honour and absolute thrill to be having the world premiere of Agata the Writer in Giornate degli Autori at the Venice Film Festival, a forum known for its belief in cinema in its most daring and surprising form,” Dorabialski and White said in a joint statement. A Whitefalk Films and Produktion Productions project, the film was executive produced by Erik Black, Wasikowska and Australian fashion brand Alémais. Screen Australia provided principal production funding, with further financial support via Creative Australia and the Adelaide Film Festival Investment Fund. Bonsai Films will handle local distribution. Agata the Writer is the second Australian project bound for Italy so far this year, with Jessica di Costa’s Mothmama selected for the main festival’s Orizzonti short films international competition. Established in 2004, Giornate degli Autori is modelled on Cannes’ Directors’ Fortnight and supported by the Italian film directors’ and authors’ associations ANAC and 100autori. Its focus is on cinema with “special care for innovation, research, originality and independence”. Dorabialski presented a 30-minute distillation of Agata the Writer, titled Field Report , at the Biennale of Sydney earlier this year. Venice Film Festival runs September 2-12. DL DovilÄ LisauskaitÄ, LRT TV, LRT.lt 2026.08.11 08:00 Vytautas the Great. Fragment from a painting by Jan Matejko, 1878 | Wikimedia Commons A nearly century-old empty sarcophagus in Vilnius Cathedral is waiting for the remains of one of Lithuaniaâs most revered rulers. This autumn, archaeologists will begin a new search for the remains of Grand Duke Vytautas the Great (c. 1350â1430), as part of a much broader effort to uncover the secrets of the cathedralâs past. The Lithuanian government approved a plan in early July for scientific research aimed at investigating possible locations of Vytautasâ remains. It also approved a wider program of research into Vilnius Cathedral, including archaeological excavations, architectural studies, historical research and the examination of human remains. The work is expected to create a database of people buried in the cathedral over different periods and a comprehensive bioarchive of samples taken from the remains. Historians and archaeologists broadly agree that the research will significantly expand knowledge of the cathedral, where systematic investigations have never been carried out on this scale. But they are divided over whether the long-standing search for Vytautasâ remains will succeed. Vilnius Cathedral | J. StaceviÄius / LRT The stone sarcophagus in the cathedralâs Chapter Crypt was made nearly 100 years ago and remains empty. Its inscription bears the date October 27, 1930, when Lithuania marked the 500th anniversary of Vytautasâ death. Vytautas, who ruled the Grand Duchy of Lithuania from 1392 until his death in 1430, never became king, although he sought a royal crown. He remains one of the most important figures in Lithuanian history. A search that began a century ago The first serious professional archaeological investigations of the cathedralâs underground crypts began around the 1930 anniversary, when researchers hoped they might find Vytautasâ intact remains, perhaps alongside his insignia or regalia. Instead, they encountered problems from the get-go. âThe reality turned out to be much more complicated because of the dampness of the underground spaces, the high groundwater level and flooding in the city,â said Alina PavasarytÄ, a historian at the Church Heritage Museum. âThe underground spaces are, obviously, underground, and this is the deepest place in the Old Town.â Alina PavasarytÄ | J. StaceviÄius / LRT Wooden coffins buried there had largely decomposed, leaving human remains mixed together, she said. The search intensified in recent years as Lithuania approaches the 600th anniversary of Vytautasâ death. It also gained momentum after historical researcher Saulius Poderis, who has been convicted of illegal archaeology, published his theory about where Vytautasâ remains might have been hidden. âI am a supporter of the theory that Vytautas was found during the interwar period,â Poderis said, arguing that systematic excavations at the cathedral at the time uncovered his remains. He points to a letter by 18th-century historian Franciszek Ksawery Bohusz, which he says indicated that Vytautas was buried near Grand Duke Alexander Jagiellon in the cathedralâs crypt. Saulius Poderis | V. Raupelis / LRT According to the official historical account, the remains of three rulers â Alexander Jagiellon, Barbara RadziwiÅÅ and Elisabeth of Austria â were discovered in the cathedral in 1931. All three are now buried in the royal crypt. Poderis argues that the remains of Vytautas may also have been discovered but deliberately concealed because Vilnius was then under Polish control and relations between Poland and Lithuania were deeply strained. âIt was a political decision. It was made on the same day the crypt was discovered,â Poderis said. A ruler turned into a national symbol Vytautasâ remains have long carried significance beyond archaeology. The 500th anniversary of his death in 1930 was one of the most important state events in interwar Lithuania. The country was still building its national identity after declaring independence in 1918, and Vytautas was embraced as a symbol of a powerful and independent Lithuania. With Vilnius under Polish control at the time, his legacy also came to symbolise Lithuaniaâs historical claim to its capital. âVytautas is remembered in Lithuanian consciousness and memory as one of the most prominent and successful rulers, a defender of independence and a symbol of Lithuania in the 14th and 15th centuries,â said Antanas Petrilionis, a lecturer at Vilnius Universityâs Faculty of History. Remains of Vytautas the Great may have been discovered in 1931, researcher says | P. Peleckis / BNS âThat image of Vytautas and his remains becomes important because people need a symbol they can see, not just hear about,â he said. Poderis said he has spent 17 years investigating the mystery and remains convinced that Vytautasâ remains were secretly reburied during the interwar period. One of the locations he considers most likely is the western wall of the royal mausoleum. Archaeologists from the Lithuanian Institute of History plan to investigate the site this autumn. The method will be deliberately limited. âThis will be an invasive investigation to check the location indicated by Poderis,â said archaeologist Rytis Jonaitis. âA hole will be drilled through the wall, a probe with a camera will be inserted and we will look at what is inside.â Poderis has identified several other possible locations. But Jonaitis said archaeologists cannot simply drill into every one. âIf we drilled into every place, we would turn the cathedral into a sieve,â he said. Ground-penetrating scans and other technologies can reveal whether there is an empty space behind a wall, Jonaitis said, but they cannot determine what is inside it. Vilnius Cathedral | E. BlaÅ¾ys / LRT A much bigger investigation The search for Vytautas is only one part of the government-backed research program. The government has allocated about 7.5 million euros for a comprehensive investigation of Vilnius Cathedral. Researchers will examine the cathedralâs history and historical documents, study its structure and masonry, conduct archaeological excavations, assess artworks and their value, and analyse human remains. Researchers believe about 800 sets of human remains have already been identified in the cathedral. But identifying Vytautas would require more than finding remains in a plausible location. Scientists would need a reliable genetic reference for comparison. âWe all know that there are about 800 sets of remains that have been discovered,â said Darius JakaviÄius, chairman of the Lithuanian parliamentâs Commission for Historical Memory. âTo begin studying them, we need what you could call a reference gene or code that we can use as a basis for comparison.â Potential DNA reference samples could come from the graves of Vytautasâ close relatives in Ukraine or the Czech Republic. Seeking a sample from Russia, where Vytautasâ only daughter, Sophia, is buried, is not currently being considered. Vytautas the Great, by Lina KalinauskaitÄ | VDU JakaviÄius said he had visited Prague and spoken with representatives of St Vitus Cathedral, where he was told there would be no obstacles to obtaining material needed for the research. Lithuaniaâs Foreign Ministry is also working on the issue, he said. Ukraine could provide another potential source of genetic material. The Pechersk Lavra in Kyiv contains the remains of prominent historical figures connected with the Grand Duchy of Lithuania and the Gediminid dynasty, JakaviÄius said. Scepticism and hope Despite the excitement surrounding the renewed search, scientists remain cautious. Asked whether he would bet on archaeologists finding Vytautasâ remains, Jonaitis said he would not. âIn science, I am an extreme sceptic,â he said. âIn my personal opinion, it is more likely that we will not find them.â JakaviÄius is more optimistic. âA year ago, there was more pessimism. Now I see more reasons for optimism,â he said. Petrilionis also expressed confidence. âI am optimistic. I think he is hiding somewhere there,â he said. Poderis, whose theory has driven much of the renewed search, stopped short of claiming certainty. âI am not saying 100%,â he said. âMy intuition has not deceived me in life. I think it wonât be empty there.â The investigation is expected to produce answers by 2030, when Lithuania will mark the 600th anniversary of Vytautasâ death. If his remains are found, the cathedral could become home to a pantheon of Lithuanian rulers. If they are not, historians say the broader investigation will still be a major success, providing a much more detailed understanding of the history of Vilnius Cathedral and the people buried beneath it. Photograph: Jim Watson/AFP/Getty Images Trump administration Trump administration planning to reimburse doctors treating vaccine ‘injury’ Experts warn that sweeping changes elevate health secretary RFK Jr’s anti-vaccine agenda and personal profit Melody Schreiber Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.00 EST Last modified on Sun 15 Nov 2026 07.02 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Trump administration is finalizing a rule to reimburse doctors who diagnose, treat and counsel patients with side effects from vaccines in what experts believe is an attempt to undermine trust in vaccines and to create an evidence base on their purported risks. Robert F Kennedy Jr, the secretary of the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), also announced the creation of a vaccine “injury” research center at the National Institutes of Health and has sought to reshape the Vaccine Injury Compensation Program (VICP) – actions that point to Kennedy’s longtime activism against vaccination as well as the profits he and his network have made from vaccine lawsuits. Kennedy and his allies have also profited from growing misinformation peddled through books, paid speaking events and the supplement industry. “I do think he’s a real ideologue – he really believes in this,” said Dorit Reiss, professor of law at UC Law San Francisco. But Kennedy and his allies are likely “very happy to make money doing it”, she said. Senator opens investigation into evidence RFK Jr ‘unlawfully lied’ to Congress Read more Peter Hotez, professor and dean of Baylor College of Medicine’s National School of Tropical Medicine, agreed, saying Kennedy’s actions are likely a combination of “being an ideological zealot and making money either for himself or for his associates”. Emily Hilliard, an HHS spokesperson, said the department “categorically reject claims that Secretary Kennedy is pursuing personal gain or seeking to dismantle American medicine”. Prior to his confirmation hearing in January 2025, Kennedy disclosed $2.5m in income from referrals for vaccine-related lawsuits. In the hearing, Kennedy would not commit to forgoing compensation from vaccine lawsuits after he leaves office. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, listed several ways in which Kennedy’s actions, some of which have now happened, could influence future litigation. “Kennedy can kill off access to vaccines and make millions of dollars while he does it,” Warren said at the hearing. “Kids might die. But Robert Kennedy can keep cashing in.” She pointed to Kennedy’s involvement in litigation against Merck for its HPV vaccine – lawsuits that were settled for more than $50m in June 2026. After the confirmation hearing, Kennedy said his son would receive the money, expected to be 10% of the total; it’s unclear if he did. “For most of us, money going to our children isn’t exactly money not going to us,” Reiss said. “There’s a dozen ways he and his family could benefit” from Kennedy’s actions, she added. Kennedy has long profited from his anti-vaccine misinformation. Tony Lyons, Kennedy’s publisher and a central figure in the constellation of Maha political organizations, reportedly paid Kennedy $4m in book advances over the past year. The publisher also paid Kennedy $451,000 in consulting fees before he became HHS secretary. That’s on top of other book sales and paid speaking engagements over the years. Kennedy also earned $326,000 for the 15 weeks he served as chairman of Children’s Health Defense in 2023 – more than half of his $510,000 salary in 2022. More recently, he received free flights and trips on a yacht from a former donor to his presidential campaign, who is now under investigation by the Senate for the gifts totaling some $250,000. As HHS secretary, Kennedy has also loosened regulations on peptides, a booming part of the largely unregulated wellness industry. “I think he’s doing what everyone knew he was going to do,” said Hotez. Kennedy, before and during his tenure as leader of HHS, has been “chipping away at public confidence in vaccines and immunizations in favor of products that can be sold by the wellness industry”, he added. Aaron Siri, Kennedy’s former lawyer who represents people who say they have experienced severe side effects, has advocated for changing all vaccines to “shared clinical decision-making”. If those changes took place, Siri could argue that the vaccines are not covered under the VICP and therefore open to litigation. “A lot of what he is doing is geared toward setting up a more profitable litigation atmosphere,” Reiss said. Siri did not respond to the Guardian’s question about profiting from litigation, but instead argued that “if vaccines are as ‘safe’ as touted by the government, then there should be no need for immunity to liability and, likewise, there should be very few, if any, successful cases”. The most common claim to VICP – making up more than half – has to do with where the vaccine is administered, not the vaccines themselves. The VICP was established in 1986 in order to expedite compensation for anyone who experienced adverse side effects from vaccines. There are real costs to undermining the program, Reiss said. It’s very rare for people to develop severe side effects after vaccination, but when they do, they should be compensated, she said. But if false claims about vaccine harms proliferate, they will obscure those with legitimate claims. Filing a VICP claim is an easier process than winning a lawsuit, which takes time and effort and also demands a higher burden of proof. “That’s why the whole vaccine injury system was set up,” Hotez said. “It was actually to the plaintiff’s benefit to get a faster judgment without having to show detailed evidence of proof.” Without VICP, patients would need to pay lawyers a large chunk of their settlements, if their case moves through the courts at all, Reiss said: “The lack of contingency fee means they don’t have to pay 30% to 50% of their earnings through the lawyer.” Compensating doctors for reporting side effects to the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System (VAERS) risks offering “the wrong incentives” to unscrupulous providers who could increase such activities to become a new revenue source, Reiss said. The changes could “certainly” be used by organizations such as Children’s Health Defense to legitimize its work spreading misinformation “and convince donors and others that they should give them more money”, she added. VAERS, alongside several other vaccine monitoring systems, works well to pick up signals of very rare side effects, such as myocarditis from initial mRNA Covid vaccines and thrombotic thrombocytopenia in the Johnson and Johnson Covid vaccine, Hotez noted. But it’s not built to prove links between vaccines and certain side effects, as vaccination opponents have attempted to do, he said. “The VAERS system was never meant to show cause and effect,” Hotez said. “It’s like looking for signs of alien communication in outer space. You look at every little blip, and almost all of them have nothing, are not real. But you have to analyze them.” Years ago, Hotez engaged Kennedy in a series of conversations about misinformation that autism spectrum disorder is related to vaccines. Hotez pointed to known environmental influences on autism, like the anti-seizure medication valproic acid. Kennedy “had no interest then; he has no interest now”, Hotez said. “Even back then, there was a heavy emphasis on being a plaintiff attorney and suing vaccine companies. So that’s his narrow interest, which has nothing to do with reality – and he’s still going by the same playbook.” Kennedy has attacked medical journals and schools, and funding for medical research has fallen sharply under his leadership. Such actions appear intended to “completely wipe out American medicine as we know it in favor of this whole system of grifting and pseudoscience”, Hotez said.
